newsitem.title: GERMANY: CDU seen winning Frankfurt vote despite econ woes.
newsitem.headline: CDU seen winning Frankfurt vote despite econ woes.

text.p: Germany's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) are expected to win a local election in the financial capital of Frankfurt next month despite presiding over record national unemployment, a survey showed on Monday.

The selection of delegates for the city parliament is part of municipal elections across the state of Hesse on March 2. The Hesse elections are the only major vote in Germany this year and Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said he will scrutinise them for clues to the outcome of next year's general election.

The opinion poll, conducted by the INRA institute in Moelln and published in Focus magazine, shows the CDU winning the vote in Frankfurt with 39 percent, up from 33.4 percent in the last election in 1993. The opposition Social Democrats score 28 percent, down from 32 percent.

INRA attributes the CDU's success in part to local infighting between the SPD and the Greens and to the popularity of its CDU mayor Petra Roth, who ousted Andreas von Schoeler of the SPD in an election in 1995.
But the survey puts the SPD narrowly ahead of the CDU at the national level.

Asked by INRA what party they would vote for if there were a general election next Sunday, 35 percent said they would vote SPD, 33 percent CDU, 16 percent the Greens and 8.5 percent the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), in coalition with the CDU in Bonn.

The Hesse elections coincide with Bonn battling to push through complex tax and pension reforms and facing heavy criticism over a level of joblessness last seen in the 1930s when Adolf Hitler came to power. Unemployment surged by more than half a million people to 4.66 million in January.
The INRA poll was conducted for Focus among 1,012 men and women in Frankfurt from February 7 through February 12.
It shows the Greens improving their share of the Frankfurt vote to 18 percent from 14 percent. The FDP is seen rising to five percent from 4.4 percent.
That is on a par with the far right Republicans, expected to see their share of the vote fall to five percent from 9.3 percent.
